headings: The fruit rule has important exceptions
raw_text:
# The Tiny Refrigerator Slider With a Big Job

A refrigerator’s crisper drawer may look like a simple storage box. But behind one small slider are two different ways to care for fresh food.

Many refrigerators offer a low-humidity choice and a high-humidity choice. The low setting lets more air move through the drawer. The high setting keeps the drawer more closed. This small design detail can affect how produce holds up over time.

Used with the right food, the drawer can help fresh produce stay in good condition longer. But the common fruit-versus-vegetable shortcut is too simple. Fresh foods do not all change in the same way.

Some foods become a problem because of what they release. Others become a problem because of what they lose. That is why the better question is not only, “Is this a fruit or a vegetable?” It is, “What does this food need most?”

## A drawer for two different problems

Think of the drawer as a small tool for two kinds of trouble. Apples and pears release ethylene, a natural gas, as they ripen. In a low-humidity drawer, air can move more easily, so the gas can leave more easily too. This can reduce the gas around nearby produce.

Leafy greens and broccoli face another problem. They can lose water quickly and wilt. A more closed, high-humidity drawer helps keep moisture around them. For an unfamiliar food, ask: what will it release or lose first?

### The fruit rule has important exceptions

A fruit is not automatically a low-humidity food. Strawberries and oranges are fruits, but they favor high humidity.

Some foods should not go in the crisper drawer at all. Tomatoes and bananas are recommended for counter storage. Potatoes, sweet potatoes, onions, and garlic need a cool, dry place instead.

So the humidity slider is only part of the decision. The food’s best storage place matters, too.

## In one line…

The small slider matters, but the bigger lesson is to follow each food’s needs—not simply its name—and to remember that some produce belongs somewhere else.

# The Small Refrigerator Slider That Changes How Fresh Food Is Kept

Open the refrigerator, and one small slider may look unimportant. But that slider changes how the crisper drawer handles fresh food.

Many refrigerators offer two choices: low humidity and high humidity. They are not simply two labels for the same space. They are two ways to store produce, and using the better setting can help food stay fresh longer.

That sounds like an easy kitchen rule: put fruit one way and vegetables the other. But that shortcut can lead you astray. The important choice is linked to the kind of food, not only its name.

A crisper drawer is less like a simple box and more like a small storage tool. It gives different foods different conditions. The question is not just, “Is this a fruit?” or “Is this a vegetable?”

It is, “What does this food need while it waits in the refrigerator?”

That small change in thinking can help you use the drawer with more care, instead of moving the slider without knowing what it does.

### Read the slider as a two-problem tool

The useful way to read the slider is to look for two different problems. Apples and pears release a natural gas called ethylene. Low humidity gives that gas a way out. Leafy greens and broccoli lose water quickly, so high humidity helps them keep moisture. For unfamiliar food, ask: what does it release, or lose, first?

### Some foods break the usual rule

Here is where the simple shortcut breaks. Strawberries and oranges are fruits, but they favor high humidity. Tomatoes and bananas are recommended for counter storage, not the drawer. Potatoes, sweet potatoes, onions, and garlic do not need refrigeration and are best kept in a cool, dry place.

## In one line…

The crisper drawer is a small tool for two different problems: what food gives off and what it loses. Choose the setting for the food, and remember that some produce belongs somewhere else.
